title: Why is using REQUIRES_NEW + synchronous REST calls to mimic a Saga an anti-pattern, and what is the correct refactor?
shortTitle: Pseudo-saga anti-pattern — REQUIRES_NEW + synchronous REST calls
topicTitle: Why is using REQUIRES_NEW + synchronous REST calls to mimic a Saga an anti-patte

s1_definition.profdef: A "pseudo-saga" holds a DB connection open in Service A while making a synchronous HTTP call to Service B over the network. The REQUIRES_NEW transaction in Service A suspends the outer TX (holding connection #1), calls Service B over REST (which may take 2-30 seconds), and only then commits. During the entire network wait, connection #1 is held — wasting a pool slot. Under load, this exhausts the connection pool even though the DB itself is healthy. It is a distributed monolith disguised as microservices. The correct refactor: flatten to REQUIRED (one connection per thread), then replace the synchronous REST call with an event-driven saga (Kafka + Transactional Outbox) or an orchestrator (Temporal/Camunda).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a teller holding one vault key open while calling another branch on the phone (REST call). The phone call takes 30 seconds. During those 30 seconds, that vault key is WASTED — nobody else can use it. If 20 tellers all call other branches simultaneously, all 20 keys are tied up on phone calls, and the vault is effectively closed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Never hold a DB connection while waiting on a network call. REQUIRES_NEW + REST = connection held during network wait = pool starvation. Refactor to event-driven saga (outbox + Kafka).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A "pseudo-saga" holds a DB connection open in Service A while making a synchronous HTTP call to Service B over the network. The REQUIRES_NEW transaction in Service A suspends the outer TX (holding connection #1), calls Service B over REST (which may take 2-30 seconds), and only then commits. During the entire network wait, connection #1 is held — wasting a pool slot. Under load, this exhausts the connection pool even though the DB itself is healthy. It is a distributed monolith disguised as microservices. The correct refactor: flatten to REQUIRED (one connection per thread), then replace the synchronous REST call with an event-driven saga (Kafka + Transactional Outbox) or an orchestrator (Temporal/Camunda).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a teller holding one vault key open while calling another branch on the phone (REST call). The phone call takes 30 seconds. During those 30 seconds, that vault key is WASTED — nobody else can use it. If 20 tellers all call other branches simultaneously, all 20 keys are tied up on phone calls, and the vault is effectively closed.

**One line to remember:** Never hold a DB connection while waiting on a network call. REQUIRES_NEW + REST = connection held during network wait = pool starvation. Refactor to event-driven saga (outbox + Kafka).

sections.s2_technical:
A pseudo-saga tries to fake distributed-transaction behavior by holding a database connection open while making a synchronous network call. Inside a `@Transactional` method the code debits the local account, then calls a partner bank over REST, and only commits after the call returns. The problem is that the connection is checked out from HikariCP for the entire method, so during the two-to-thirty-second network wait the connection is held but idle on the database side. Adding `REQUIRES_NEW` makes it worse, because the outer transaction's connection is suspended while a second connection is used — so one request can pin two connections.

Under load this starves the pool. With twenty connections and a three-second partner call, throughput is capped at roughly seven requests per second; beyond that, requests fail with "Connection is not available" even though the database is perfectly healthy. This is a distributed monolith disguised as microservices. The correct refactor is to make the transaction do database work only and keep it short, then move the network call outside the transaction. The durable way to do that is the Transactional Outbox: write the business row and an outbox event in the same short transaction, commit, and let a relay publish the event to Kafka so a separate consumer performs the partner call. For example, instead of `@Transactional { debit(); partnerApi.call(); }` you write `@Transactional { debit(); outbox.save(event); }` and handle the partner call asynchronously. A senior nuance: this trades strict atomicity for eventual consistency, which is the right choice across service boundaries.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's cross-border transfer service debits the local account, then calls the partner bank's API (REST) to credit the foreign account.** The developer wrapped both in REQUIRES_NEW transactions, holding the DB connection open for the entire duration of the REST call (2-5 seconds). Under 20 concurrent transfers, all 20 HikariCP connections are held during network waits. The pool is exhausted. New requests fail with "Connection not available." The DB is idle — the bottleneck is the network call holding connections.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Rs.5,000 cross-border transfer from Rajesh (SAV2001) to IBAN DE89..., where the partner bank API takes 3 seconds.

**Step 1.** In the good service, the `@Transactional` method begins and checks out one HikariCP connection. It records the transfer with status PENDING_PARTNER.

**Step 2.** In the SAME transaction it writes an outbox event describing the required partner credit. No network call happens here, so the connection is used only for about 10 milliseconds of database work.

**Step 3.** The transaction commits and the connection is immediately returned to the pool. The HTTP response goes back to Rajesh right away with status PENDING_PARTNER — no waiting on the partner.

**Step 4.** A separate outbox relay polls for unpublished events and publishes them to Kafka. A partner-integration consumer picks up the event and makes the 3-second REST call to the partner bank, holding its own connection only briefly for the final status update.

**Step 5.** When the partner confirms, the consumer updates the transfer to COMPLETED. Throughput is no longer capped by the network because connections are held for milliseconds of DB work, not seconds of waiting — roughly 2000 requests per second instead of 7.

```
INFO  [exec-1] GoodTransferService - transfer PENDING_PARTNER + outbox event (TX ~10ms), COMMIT
INFO  [relay-1] OutboxRelay - published CROSS_BORDER_INITIATED to Kafka
INFO  [consumer-1] PartnerConsumer - partner API 3s → transfer COMPLETED (own short TX)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ ANTI-PATTERN: Pseudo-saga (REQUIRES_NEW + REST) ═══

  @Transactional
  transferBad():
    ├─ Connection #1 acquired from HikariCP
    ├─ INSERT transfer (5ms)
    ├─ partnerClient.creditForeignAccount() ← 3000ms NETWORK CALL
    │   ├─ Connection #1 HELD during entire wait!
    │   ├─ DB is IDLE — connection is WASTED on network
    │   └─ 20 connections × 3s = max 7 req/s throughput
    ├─ UPDATE transfer (5ms)
    └─ COMMIT + release connection (3010ms total hold time!)

  Under load (10 req/s):
    → Pool exhausted in 6 seconds
    → "Connection is not available" errors
    → DB is healthy but app is broken = DISTRIBUTED MONOLITH

  ═══ CORRECT: Event-driven saga (outbox) ═══

  @Transactional
  transferGood():
    ├─ Connection #1 acquired
    ├─ INSERT transfer (5ms)
    ├─ INSERT outbox event (5ms) ← SAME TX as transfer
    └─ COMMIT + release connection (10ms total hold time!)

  Outbox relay (separate process, separate connection):
    ├─ Poll outbox_events WHERE published=FALSE
    ├─ Publish to Kafka topic: "cross-border-events"
    └─ Partner integration consumer:
        ├─ Gets own connection (if needed)
        ├─ Calls partnerClient.creditForeignAccount() (3000ms)
        ├─ Updates transfer status → COMPLETED
        └─ Connection held only for UPDATE (5ms), NOT during network call

  Throughput: 20 connections / 0.01s = 2000 req/s (vs 7 req/s) — 285× improvement!

  ═══ RULE ═══
  NEVER hold a DB connection while waiting on a network call.
  TX should contain ONLY DB operations.
  External calls happen OUTSIDE the TX via events/outbox/async.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The pseudo-saga anti-pattern holds a database connection open while making a synchronous REST call to another service. REQUIRES_NEW makes it worse by holding TWO connections. The connection is wasted during the entire network wait — the database is idle but the pool slot is occupied. With 20 connections and a 3-second partner API call, maximum throughput is only 7 transfers per second. At any higher rate, the pool exhausts and the application fails even though the database is perfectly healthy.

In my cross-border transfer service, the correct refactor replaces the synchronous REST call inside the transaction with a transactional outbox pattern. The transaction contains only database operations: save the transfer and write an outbox event in the same transaction — 10 milliseconds total, then the connection is released. A separate outbox relay process publishes the event to Kafka, and a partner integration consumer makes the slow REST call with its own connection held only for the response update. Throughput jumps from 7 to 2000 transfers per second — a 285x improvement — because connections are held for milliseconds of actual DB work instead of seconds of network waiting. The rule is: never hold a database connection while waiting on a network call. Transactions should contain only database operations.
